Pick one world—Frontier Settlement, Investigation Bureau,\nStarship Log, or Small Business—and let useful course capabilities serve the\nworld rather than forcing a checklist.\n\nWeek 2 permits only light, ungraded genre/world seeding. The first graded\nbuild begins Week 3.\n\n## Growth path\n\n| Weeks | Purpose | Required evidence |\n|---|---|---|\n| 3–4 | S01 sound collaborating objects, composition, invariants | bounded build, test/trace, boundary rationale |\n| 5 | S02 earned inheritance/polymorphism | real substitution or reason composition fits better |\n| 6 | S03 contracts | swappable collaborator, contract test, explanation |\n| 7–8 | S05/S06 data abstractions and tradeoffs | world-fit list/stack/queue flow and search/order reasoning |\n| 9 | S04 compact GUI/events | thin Tkinter model/view feature, meaningful callback, and independent model test/trace |\n| 10 | S09 visualization | real world/project data, question, honest readable visual, chart-choice rationale |\n| 11 | S09 storytelling / flex | evidence-backed claim, limitation/uncertainty, and a design/operational decision; deeper structures optional |\n| 12–13 | S08 stabilization and culmination | tests, docs, design review, usable/recoverable project |\n| 14 | S08 workflow/reproducibility | history/recovery/collaboration/AI-review receipt; containers only after environment verification |\n\nA gate must fit the selected world. No universal hierarchy, recursion, chart,\nor search/sort checklist exists. Examples include settlement services, case\nworkflows, ship operations, and business inventory/transactions; each can use\ncomposition, a contract, a data abstraction, or a modest interface without\nartificial symmetry.\n\n## World Bible\n\nKeep a short living project record: charter, current state, one line per week\nsaying what changed/broke, known debt, tests/evidence, and important design\nchoices. Read from input the number of people attending, the average number of slices per person and the cost of one pizza. Dollar values are output with two decimals. For example,<span>&nbsp;</span><code>print(f\\\"Cost: ${cost:.2f}\\\")</code>.<br><br>Note: this program is designed for<span>&nbsp;</span><em>incremental development</em>. Complete each step and submit for grading before starting the next step. Only a portion of tests pass after each step but confirm progress.</p><p><strong>Step 1 (2 pts).</strong><span>&nbsp;</span>Read from input the number of people (int), average slices per person (float) and cost of one pizza (float). Hint: Use the ceil() function from the math library to round up to the nearest whole number and convert to an int. Calculate and output the cost for all pizzas. Submit for grading to confirm test 1 passes.<br>Ex: If the input is:</p><pre><code>10  2.6  10.50\\n</code></pre><p>The output is:</p><pre><code>Friday Night Party\\n4 Pizzas: $42.00\\n</code></pre><p><br><strong>Step 2 (2 pts).</strong><span>&nbsp;</span>Calculate and output the sales tax (7%). Calculate and output the delivery charge (20% of cost including tax). Submit for grading to confirm 2 tests pass.<br>Ex: If the input is:</p><pre><code>10  2.6  10.50\\n</code></pre><p>The output is:</p><pre><code>Friday Night Party\\n4 Pizzas: $42.00\\nTax: $2.94\\nDelivery: $8.99\\n</code></pre><p><br><strong>Step 3 (2 pts).</strong><span>&nbsp;</span>Calculate and output the total including pizza, tax and delivery. Submit for grading to confirm 3 tests pass.<br>Ex: If the input is:</p><pre><code>10  2.6  10.50\\n</code></pre><p>The output is:</p><pre><code>Friday Night Party\\n4 Pizzas: $42.00\\nTax: $2.94\\nDelivery: $8.99\\nTotal: $53.93\\n</code></pre><p><br><strong>Step 4 (2 pts).</strong><span>&nbsp;</span>Repeat steps 1 - 3 with additional inputs for Saturday night (one order per line). Maintain and output a separate total for both parties. Unlike a<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Compare output test</em>, which evaluates your program's output for specific input values, a<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Unit test</em><span>&nbsp;</span>evaluates individual functions to determines if each function:</p>\\n<ul>\\n<li>is named correctly and has the correct parameters and return type</li>\\n<li>calculates and returns the correct value (or prints the correct output)</li>\\n</ul>\\n<p>The zyLabs auto-grader runs<span>&nbsp;</span><strong>main.py</strong><span>&nbsp;</span>as a script. In<span>&nbsp;</span><strong>main.py</strong>, the line<span>&nbsp;</span><code>if __name__ == '__main__':</code><span>&nbsp;</span>is used to separate the main code from the functions' code so that each function can be unit tested. Enter statements to be run as the main code under<span>&nbsp;</span><code>if __name__ == '__main__':</code>. Indent the statements so the statements belong to the if block. Refer to the subsection<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Importing modules and executing scripts</em><span>&nbsp;</span>under section<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Module basics</em><span>&nbsp;</span>for more information about running a program as a script.</p>\\n<p>Note: Do not remove<span>&nbsp;</span><code>if __name__ == '__main__':</code><span>&nbsp;</span>from the code. Otherwise, the unit tests will fail even though the program produces the correct output.</p>\\n<p>This example lab uses multiple unit tests to test the kilo_to_pounds() function.</p>\\n<hr>\\n<p>Complete a program that takes a weight in kilograms as input, converts the weight to pounds, and then outputs the weight in pounds. 1 kilogram = 2.204 pounds (lbs).</p>\\n<p>The program must define the following function:<br><code>def kilo_to_pounds(kilos)</code><span>&nbsp;</span>- take<span>&nbsp;</span><code>kilos</code><span>&nbsp;</span>as a parameter, convert<span>&nbsp;</span><code>kilos</code><span>&nbsp;</span>from kilograms to pounds, and return the weight in pounds.</p>\\n<p>Ex: If the input of the program is:</p>\\n<pre><code>10\\n</code></pre>\\n<p>10 is passed to kilo_to_pounds() and the output of the program is:</p>\\n<pre><code>22.040 lbs\\n</code></pre>\\n<hr>\\n<p>The program below has an error in the kilo_to_pounds() function.</p>\\n<ol>\\n<li>\\n<p>Try submitting the program for grading (click \\\"Submit mode\\\", then \\\"Submit for grading\\\"). Notice that the first two test cases fail, but the third test case passes. The first test case fails because the program outputs the result from the kilo_to_pounds() function, which has an error. The second test case uses a<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Unit test</em><span>&nbsp;</span>to test the kilo_to_pounds() function, which fails.</p>\\n</li>\\n<li>\\n<p>Change the kilo_to_pounds() function to multiply the variable kilos by 2.204, instead of dividing. The return statement should be:<span>&nbsp;</span><code>return (kilos * 2.204)</code>. Submit again. Now the test cases should all pass.</p>\\n</li>\\n</ol>\\n<p>Note: A<span>&nbsp;</span><u>common error</u><span>&nbsp;</span>is to mistype a function name with the incorrect capitalization. Function names are case sensitive, so if a lab program asks for a kilo_to_pounds() function, a kilo_To_Pounds() function that works for you in \\\"Develop mode\\\" will result in a failed unit test. The unit test will not be able to find kilo_to_pounds().</p>\\n</div>\\n</div>\\n</div>\\n<p># Starter Code :</p>\\n<p>def kilo_to_pounds(kilos):<br>&nbsp; &nbsp; # This statement intentionally has an error.&nbsp;<br>&nbsp; &nbsp; return (kilos / 2.204)</p>\\n<p><br># Main part of the program starts here. Do not remove the line below.<br>if __name__ == '__main__':<br>&nbsp; &nbsp; kilos = float(input())<br>&nbsp; &nbsp;&nbsp;<br>&nbsp; &nbsp; pounds = kilo_to_pounds(kilos)<br>&nbsp; &nbsp; print(f'{pounds:.3f} lbs')</p>\\n<p># Problem : )</p>\\n<div class=\\\"flex flex-row items-center\\\">\\n<h1 class=\\\"zybook-section-title\\\">6.19<span>&nbsp;</span>LAB: Driving costs - functions</h1>\\n</div>\\n<div class=\\\"section-content-resources-container\\\">\\n<div id=\\\"ember19\\\" class=\\\"content-resource markdown-content-resource markdown-content-resource ember-view\\\">\\n<div id=\\\"ember20\\\" class=\\\"ember-view\\\">\\n<p>Write a function driving_cost() with input parameters miles_per_gallon, dollars_per_gallon, and miles_driven, that returns the dollar cost to drive those miles.     \"body\": \"\\n\\n\\n  \\n  \\n  Lecture Module: Scarcity vs Surplus (Abundance) \\u2014 What Fear Does to the Mind\\n  \\n\\n\\n\\n  <h1>Lecture Module: Scarcity vs Surplus (Abundance) \\u2014 What Fear Does to the Mind</h1>\\n  <p class=\\\"meta\\\"><strong>Audience:</strong> Humans (especially CS students under deadline pressure)<br>\\n  <strong>Purpose:</strong> Explain scarcity mindset vs surplus mindset, why each happens, how it affects cognition, and how to build healthier habits without ignoring real constraints.</p>\\n\\n  <hr>\\n\\n  <h2>1) The Core Question</h2>\\n  <p>\\n    Why do some people live like the world is always about to run out\\u2014time, money, attention, love, safety\\u2014while others\\n    move through life like there will be enough, and so they can be generous?\\n  </p>\\n  <p>\\n    This isn\\u2019t just \\u201cattitude.\\u201d It\\u2019s often <strong>nervous system + history + environment + learned strategy</strong>.\\n  </p>\\n\\n  <h2>2) Definitions (simple and useful)</h2>\\n\\n  <h3>Scarcity mindset</h3>\\n  <p>A mental state where the brain is convinced:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li><strong>there won\\u2019t be enough</strong></li>\\n    <li><strong>I have to protect what I have</strong></li>\\n    <li><strong>if I relax, I\\u2019ll lose</strong></li>\\n    <li><strong>if I fall behind, I won\\u2019t recover</strong></li>\\n  </ul>\\n  <p>\\n    Scarcity can be triggered by real conditions (poverty, instability, trauma, illness), or by perceived conditions\\n    (comparison, uncertainty, perfectionism, high-stakes environments).\\n  </p>\\n\\n  <h3>Surplus (abundance) mindset</h3>\\n  <p>A mental state where the brain is convinced:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li><strong>I can recover</strong></li>\\n    <li><strong>resources can be replenished</strong></li>\\n    <li><strong>I can share without collapsing</strong></li>\\n    <li><strong>I have enough margin to breathe and think</strong></li>\\n  </ul>\\n  <p>Surplus is not \\u201cdelusion.\\u201d It\\u2019s <strong>felt safety + margin + trust</strong>.</p>\\n\\n  <h2>3) What Scarcity Does to the Mind (the \\u201ctunnel\\u201d effect)</h2>\\n  <p>When people feel scarcity, the brain does something predictable:</p>\\n\\n  <h3>3.1 Attention tunnels</h3>\\n  <p>Scarcity pulls attention toward the \\u201curgent threat\\u201d:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>\\u201cI\\u2019m behind.\\u201d</li>\\n    <li>\\u201cI\\u2019m going to fail.\\u201d</li>\\n    <li>\\u201cI\\u2019m running out of time.\\u201d</li>\\n    <li>\\u201cI can\\u2019t mess this up.\\u201d</li>\\n  </ul>\\n  <p>This tunneling can create:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>hyper-focus on immediate tasks</li>\\n    <li>difficulty seeing long-term plans</li>\\n    <li>reduced ability to switch contexts cleanly</li>\\n  </ul>\\n\\n  <h3>3.2 Working memory shrinks</h3>\\n  <p>\\n    Fear eats mental bandwidth. It\\u2019s like trying to debug while your computer is also running a full virus scan.\\n  </p>\\n  <p>Symptoms:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>forgetting steps</li>\\n    <li>losing track of what you tried</li>\\n    <li>rereading the same paragraph 6 times</li>\\n    <li>making impulsive choices just to end discomfort</li>\\n  </ul>\\n\\n  <h3>3.3 Executive function gets expensive</h3>\\n  <p>\\n    Planning, prioritizing, and resisting distraction require energy. Scarcity makes those skills cost more.\\n  </p>\\n  <p>So people default to:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>quick rewards (scrolling, snacking, distractions)</li>\\n    <li>avoidance (\\u201cI\\u2019ll start later\\u201d)</li>\\n    <li>over-control (perfectionism, micromanaging)</li>\\n  </ul>\\n\\n  <h3>3.4 Social behavior contracts</h3>\\n  <p>\\n    Scarcity often reduces generosity\\u2014not because someone is selfish, but because the brain says:\\n  </p>\\n  <div class=\\\"callout\\\"><strong>\\u201cIf I give, I might not survive.\\u201d</strong></div>\\n  <p>This can look like:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>less patience</li>\\n    <li>less collaboration</li>\\n    <li>more defensiveness</li>\\n    <li>more \\u201ckeeping score\\u201d</li>\\n  </ul>\\n\\n  <h3>3.5 The cruel loop</h3>\\n  <p>\\n    Scarcity makes it harder to make good decisions, which can lead to worse outcomes, which increases scarcity.\\n  </p>\\n  <p>That loop is why shame is such a bad teacher.</p>\\n\\n  <h2>4) What Surplus Does to the Mind (the \\u201cwide angle\\u201d effect)</h2>\\n\\n  <h3>4.1 Cognitive flexibility increases</h3>\\n  <p>Surplus supports:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>creativity</li>\\n    <li>learning</li>\\n    <li>problem-solving</li>\\n    <li>perspective-taking</li>\\n  </ul>\\n  <p>You can hold multiple ideas without panicking.</p>\\n\\n  <h3>4.2 Long-term planning becomes possible</h3>\\n  <p>Surplus makes it easier to:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>start early</li>\\n    <li>break tasks into chunks</li>\\n    <li>recover from mistakes</li>\\n    <li>invest in skills that pay off later</li>\\n  </ul>\\n\\n  <h3>4.3 Generosity becomes rational</h3>\\n  <p>\\n    When you trust you can recover, generosity stops feeling like danger.\\n    You can share time, attention, knowledge, encouragement, and resources.\\n  </p>\\n  <p>\\n    And generosity tends to strengthen relationships\\u2014which increases support\\u2014which increases felt surplus.\\n    That\\u2019s the \\u201cgood spiral.\\u201d\\n  </p>\\n\\n  <h2>5) Why Surplus is a Good Idea (and also why it\\u2019s hard)</h2>\\n\\n  <h3>Why it\\u2019s a good idea</h3>\\n  <p>Surplus mindset tends to produce:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>better thinking</li>\\n    <li>better relationships</li>\\n    <li>better resilience after failure</li>\\n    <li>more consistent progress</li>\\n    <li>less desperation-driven decision-making</li>\\n  </ul>\\n  <p>In a CS context, surplus supports the ability to calmly do the real work:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>read carefully</li>\\n    <li>test hypotheses</li>\\n    <li>debug systematically</li>\\n    <li>ask for help early</li>\\n    <li>collaborate without ego fights</li>\\n  </ul>\\n\\n  <h3>Why it\\u2019s a challenge</h3>\\n  <p>Surplus isn\\u2019t a slogan. It requires at least one of these:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li><strong>Real resources</strong> (money, time, stable housing, reliable support)</li>\\n    <li><strong>Real margin</strong> (buffers, slack, recovery plans)</li>\\n    <li><strong>Real safety</strong> (psychological safety, predictable rules, dignity)</li>\\n    <li><strong>Real repetition</strong> (evidence that \\u201cI can recover\\u201d becomes believable)</li>\\n  </ul>\\n  <p>\\n    If a person is truly in scarcity, telling them \\u201cjust think abundant thoughts\\u201d can feel insulting.\\n    Surplus mindset is easiest when the environment supports it.\\n  </p>\\n\\n  <h2>6) The Big Warning: Don\\u2019t turn \\u201cabundance\\u201d into blame</h2>\\n  <p>\\n    Some people are in real, structural scarcity. They are not \\u201cfailing at mindset.\\u201d\\n    They are adapting to reality.\\n  </p>\\n  <p>\\n    A healthy classroom message is:\\n  </p>\\n  <div class=\\\"callout\\\">\\n    \\u201cWe respect real constraints.<br>\\n    We build tiny buffers where we can.<br>\\n    We avoid creating unnecessary threat.<br>\\n    We practice surplus in ways that don\\u2019t deny reality.\\u201d\\n  </div>\\n\\n  <h2>7) How Students Can Start Building Surplus (even if life is chaotic)</h2>\\n  <p>Surplus begins with <strong>micro-margin</strong>: tiny pockets of safety.</p>\\n\\n  <h3>7.1 The \\u201cHalf-Breath + Wide-Angle\\u201d reset (10 seconds)</h3>\\n  <ol>\\n    <li>Exhale slightly longer than normal</li>\\n    <li>Look away from the screen and notice <strong>three things</strong> in the room</li>\\n    <li>Ask: <strong>\\u201cWhat is the smallest next action?\\u201d</strong></li>\\n  </ol>\\n  <p>This interrupts tunnel vision.</p>\\n\\n  <h3>7.2 Build a 15-minute \\u201cbuffer block\\u201d</h3>\\n  <p>Once per day, schedule <strong>15 minutes</strong> that is not for doing tasks\\u2014only for:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>planning tomorrow</li>\\n    <li>catching up on one tiny thing</li>\\n    <li>asking one question</li>\\n    <li>cleaning one mess</li>\\n    <li>making one \\u201cfuture me\\u201d gift</li>\\n  </ul>\\n  <p>This is how you manufacture margin in a life that doesn\\u2019t provide it.</p>\\n\\n  <h3>7.3 The \\u201cGenerosity without collapse\\u201d rule</h3>\\n  <p>Generosity doesn\\u2019t mean draining yourself dry. Teach students to be generous <strong>with boundaries</strong>.</p>\\n  <p>Offer help in small, repeatable units:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>\\u201cI can help for 10 minutes.\\u201d</li>\\n    <li>\\u201cI can explain one concept.\\u201d</li>\\n    <li>\\u201cI can review one function.\\u201d</li>\\n    <li>\\u201cI can point you to the right resource.\\u201d</li>\\n  </ul>\\n\\n  <h3>7.4 Replace \\u201cI\\u2019m behind\\u201d with \\u201cWhat\\u2019s next\\u201d</h3>\\n  <p>\\u201cI\\u2019m behind\\u201d is a scarcity spell. \\u201cWhat\\u2019s next\\u201d is a surplus question.</p>\\n\\n  <h3>7.5 The anti-scarcity workflow for assignments</h3>\\n  <ol>\\n    <li>Define \\u201cdone for now\\u201d</li>\\n    <li>Find the smallest deliverable</li>\\n    <li>Do one short sprint (Pomodoro or mini-sprint)</li>\\n    <li>Leave a \\u201cresume hook\\u201d (one sentence: \\u201cNext I will\\u2026\\u201d) </li>\\n  </ol>\\n  <p>Consistency builds safety.</p>\\n\\n  <h2>8) Teaching this to CS majors (how to make it land)</h2>\\n\\n  <h3>8.1 Translate into systems language</h3>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>Scarcity = low bandwidth, high interrupt load, no cache, constant paging</li>\\n    <li>Surplus = enough RAM to reason, plan, and run multiple processes safely</li>\\n  </ul>\\n\\n  <h3>8.2 Reward process artifacts (not panic hours)</h3>\\n  <p>Ask for:</p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>commits</li>\\n    <li>test logs</li>\\n    <li>short debug journals (\\u201chypothesis \\u2192 experiment \\u2192 result\\u201d)</li>\\n    <li>checklists</li>\\n  </ul>\\n  <p>That reduces the \\u201call-or-nothing\\u201d scarcity vibe.</p>\\n\\n  <h3>8.3 Don\\u2019t weaponize deadlines</h3>\\n  <p>\\n    Deadlines matter, but \\u201cdoom language\\u201d spikes tunnel vision.\\n    Use predictable rules + recovery paths:\\n  </p>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>partial credit for early drafts</li>\\n    <li>revision windows</li>\\n    <li>checkpoints</li>\\n    <li>clear rubrics</li>\\n  </ul>\\n  <p>This encourages learning rather than hiding.</p>\\n\\n  <h2>9) Discussion prompts</h2>\\n  <ul>\\n    <li>Where do you feel scarcity most: time, money, attention, belonging, confidence?</li>\\n    <li>What does scarcity make you do that you later regret?</li>\\n    <li>What does surplus make possible in your best weeks?</li>\\n    <li>What\\u2019s one tiny buffer you could build this week?</li>\\n    <li>What is a generous action you can take that won\\u2019t collapse you?</li>\\n  </ul>\\n\\n  <h2>10) A short closing script</h2>\\n  <div class=\\\"callout\\\">\\n    \\u201cScarcity makes the mind tunnel.<br>\\n    Surplus gives the mind a wide lens.<br><br>\\n    We\\u2019re not pretending life is easy.<br>\\n    We\\u2019re building tiny pockets of margin\\u2014so our brains can do what they do best: learn, solve, and connect.<br><br>\\n    Your goal is not to become endlessly calm.<br>\\n    Your goal is to become <strong>recoverable</strong>.<br>\\n    When you believe you can recover, you can be brave.<br>\\n    And when you can be brave, you can build.\\u201d\\n  </div>\\n\\n  <hr>\\n  <p Unlike a<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Compare output test</em>, which evaluates your program's output for specific input values, a<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Unit test</em><span>&nbsp;</span>evaluates individual functions to determines if each function:</p>\\n<ul>\\n<li>is named correctly and has the correct parameters and return type</li>\\n<li>calculates and returns the correct value (or prints the correct output)</li>\\n</ul>\\n<p>The zyLabs auto-grader runs<span>&nbsp;</span><strong>main.py</strong><span>&nbsp;</span>as a script. In<span>&nbsp;</span><strong>main.py</strong>, the line<span>&nbsp;</span><code>if __name__ == '__main__':</code><span>&nbsp;</span>is used to separate the main code from the functions' code so that each function can be unit tested. Enter statements to be run as the main code under<span>&nbsp;</span><code>if __name__ == '__main__':</code>. Indent the statements so the statements belong to the if block. Refer to the subsection<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Importing modules and executing scripts</em><span>&nbsp;</span>under section<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Module basics</em><span>&nbsp;</span>for more information about running a program as a script.</p>\\n<p>Note: Do not remove<span>&nbsp;</span><code>if __name__ == '__main__':</code><span>&nbsp;</span>from the code. Otherwise, the unit tests will fail even though the program produces the correct output.</p>\\n<p>This example lab uses multiple unit tests to test the kilo_to_pounds() function.</p>\\n<hr>\\n<p>Complete a program that takes a weight in kilograms as input, converts the weight to pounds, and then outputs the weight in pounds. 1 kilogram = 2.204 pounds (lbs).</p>\\n<p>The program must define the following function:<br><code>def kilo_to_pounds(kilos)</code><span>&nbsp;</span>- take<span>&nbsp;</span><code>kilos</code><span>&nbsp;</span>as a parameter, convert<span>&nbsp;</span><code>kilos</code><span>&nbsp;</span>from kilograms to pounds, and return the weight in pounds.</p>\\n<p>Ex: If the input of the program is:</p>\\n<pre><code>10\\n</code></pre>\\n<p>10 is passed to kilo_to_pounds() and the output of the program is:</p>\\n<pre><code>22.040 lbs\\n</code></pre>\\n<hr>\\n<p>The program below has an error in the kilo_to_pounds() function.</p>\\n<ol>\\n<li>\\n<p>Try submitting the program for grading (click \\\"Submit mode\\\", then \\\"Submit for grading\\\"). Notice that the first two test cases fail, but the third test case passes. The first test case fails because the program outputs the result from the kilo_to_pounds() function, which has an error. The second test case uses a<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Unit test</em><span>&nbsp;</span>to test the kilo_to_pounds() function, which fails.</p>\\n</li>\\n<li>\\n<p>Change the kilo_to_pounds() function to multiply the variable kilos by 2.204, instead of dividing. The return statement should be:<span>&nbsp;</span><code>return (kilos * 2.204)</code>. Submit again. Now the test cases should all pass.</p>\\n</li>\\n</ol>\\n<p>Note: A<span>&nbsp;</span><u>common error</u><span>&nbsp;</span>is to mistype a function name with the incorrect capitalization. Function names are case sensitive, so if a lab program asks for a kilo_to_pounds() function, a kilo_To_Pounds() function that works for you in \\\"Develop mode\\\" will result in a failed unit test. The unit test will not be able to find kilo_to_pounds().</p>\\n</div>\\n</div>\\n</div>\\n<p># Starter Code :</p>\\n<p>def kilo_to_pounds(kilos):<br>&nbsp; &nbsp; # This statement intentionally has an error.&nbsp;<br>&nbsp; &nbsp; return (kilos / 2.204)</p>\\n<p><br># Main part of the program starts here. Unlike a<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Compare output test</em>, which evaluates your program's output for specific input values, a<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Unit test</em><span>&nbsp;</span>evaluates individual functions to determines if each function:</p>\\n<ul>\\n<li>is named correctly and has the correct parameters and return type</li>\\n<li>calculates and returns the correct value (or prints the correct output)</li>\\n</ul>\\n<p>The zyLabs auto-grader runs<span>&nbsp;</span><strong>main.py</strong><span>&nbsp;</span>as a script. In<span>&nbsp;</span><strong>main.py</strong>, the line<span>&nbsp;</span><code>if __name__ == '__main__':</code><span>&nbsp;</span>is used to separate the main code from the functions' code so that each function can be unit tested. Enter statements to be run as the main code under<span>&nbsp;</span><code>if __name__ == '__main__':</code>. Indent the statements so the statements belong to the if block. Refer to the subsection<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Importing modules and executing scripts</em><span>&nbsp;</span>under section<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Module basics</em><span>&nbsp;</span>for more information about running a program as a script.</p>\\n<p>Note: Do not remove<span>&nbsp;</span><code>if __name__ == '__main__':</code><span>&nbsp;</span>from the code. Otherwise, the unit tests will fail even though the program produces the correct output.</p>\\n<p>This example lab uses multiple unit tests to test the kilo_to_pounds() function.</p>\\n<hr>\\n<p>Complete a program that takes a weight in kilograms as input, converts the weight to pounds, and then outputs the weight in pounds. 1 kilogram = 2.204 pounds (lbs).</p>\\n<p>The program must define the following function:<br><code>def kilo_to_pounds(kilos)</code><span>&nbsp;</span>- take<span>&nbsp;</span><code>kilos</code><span>&nbsp;</span>as a parameter, convert<span>&nbsp;</span><code>kilos</code><span>&nbsp;</span>from kilograms to pounds, and return the weight in pounds.</p>\\n<p>Ex: If the input of the program is:</p>\\n<pre><code>10\\n</code></pre>\\n<p>10 is passed to kilo_to_pounds() and the output of the program is:</p>\\n<pre><code>22.040 lbs\\n</code></pre>\\n<hr>\\n<p>The program below has an error in the kilo_to_pounds() function.</p>\\n<ol>\\n<li>\\n<p>Try submitting the program for grading (click \\\"Submit mode\\\", then \\\"Submit for grading\\\"). Notice that the first two test cases fail, but the third test case passes. The first test case fails because the program outputs the result from the kilo_to_pounds() function, which has an error. The second test case uses a<span>&nbsp;</span><em>Unit test</em><span>&nbsp;</span>to test the kilo_to_pounds() function, which fails.</p>\\n</li>\\n<li>\\n<p>Change the kilo_to_pounds() function to multiply the variable kilos by 2.204, instead of dividing. The return statement should be:<span>&nbsp;</span><code>return (kilos * 2.204)</code>. Submit again. class=\\\"activity-payload\\\">\\n<div class=\\\"fr-view\\\">\\n<p>Complete the functions in the template to implement the formulas shown below.</p>\\n<p>The formula to calculate how much of a radioactive isotope with half-life T will remain after time t is:</p>\\n<p>N_t * e ^ ((-0.693 * t )/ T)</p>\\n<p><span>The formula can be rearranged to calculate the half-life of an isotope given how much remains after decay:</span></p>\\n<p>&nbsp;</p>\\n<p><span>T = (-0.693 * t) / Natural_log(N_t/N_0)</span></p>\\n<p>The notation used in the formulas is:</p>\\n<ul>\\n<li>e = Euler's number</li>\\n<li>t = the length of time (in years) during which an isotope decays</li>\\n<li>T = the half-life (in years) of the isotope</li>\\n<li>N<sub>0</sub><span>&nbsp;</span>= the initial amount of the isotope</li>\\n<li>N<sub>t</sub><span>&nbsp;</span>the amount of the isotope remaining after time t</li>\\n</ul>\\n<p>Then, complete the main program to:</p>\\n<ol>\\n<li>Read a choice</li>\\n<li>Read 3 numbers from one line:\\n<ul>\\n<li>Choice N: N0, t, and T</li>\\n<li>Choice T: N0, Nt, and t</li>\\n</ul>\\n</li>\\n<li>Call compute_Nt() if the choice is N, compute_T if the choice is T</li>\\n<li>Output the result with four digits after the decimal point.</li>\\n</ol>\\n<p><em>Note: Use math.exp() to calculate the exponential value with the base set to e.</em></p>\\n<p>Ex: If the input is:</p>\\n<pre><code>N\\n100 50 28.94\\n</code></pre>\\n<p>the output is:</p>\\n<pre><code>Nt = 30.2007\\n</code></pre>\\n<p>Ex: If the input
